title: Zigzag Down the Diagonals
statement:
You get an m × n grid of integers. Read it one anti-diagonal at a time, where diagonal d holds every cell with row + col = d, for d = 0, 1, 2, ….

The direction alternates. On even diagonals read upward (row decreasing, from bottom-left to top-right). On odd diagonals read downward (row increasing, from top-right to bottom-left). Return all values in that order.

examples.why: Diagonal 1 goes down: 2 then 4. Diagonal 2 goes up and starts at the bottom row: 5 then 3.
A tall grid: diagonal 2 starts at row 2 (5) and climbs to 4. Diagonal 3 starts at row 2 because column 3 does not exist.
A single row: every diagonal has one cell, so direction does not matter.

hints: Every cell on one diagonal has the same row + col. How many diagonals are there?
Collect each diagonal top to bottom, then reverse the even ones before appending. That is already linear.
To do it without buffers, compute where each diagonal starts: for an upward diagonal d the first row is min(d, m − 1); for a downward one the first column is min(d, n − 1).

explain.intuition:
Cells on the same anti-diagonal share row + col, and there are m + n − 1 diagonals. If you read each diagonal top to bottom, the zigzag is just "reverse every other one". That version is easy to get right and runs in linear time with one temporary list per diagonal.

The direct walk avoids the reversal by starting each diagonal at the right end. An upward diagonal starts at the lowest row that exists, min(d, m − 1), with col = d − row, and walks while both coordinates stay in the grid. A downward one starts at the rightmost column, min(d, n − 1). Clamping the start is the whole trick; the edges of a wide or tall grid are where hand-written bounce rules usually break.
steps: If d is even, set row = min(d, m − 1), col = d − row, and while row ≥ 0 and col < n append the cell, then row−−, col++.
If d is odd, set col = min(d, n − 1), row = d − col, and while col ≥ 0 and row < m append the cell, then row++, col−−.
pitfalls: Starting an upward diagonal at row d when d ≥ m. Clamp it to the last row.
Bounce rules that check the top edge before the right edge at the top-right corner, which sends the walk off the grid.
Mixing up which direction goes first: diagonal 0 has one cell, so the first real choice is diagonal 1, which goes down.

solutions.title: Bucket by row + col, reverse the even ones
solutions.idea: Collect every diagonal top to bottom, then append the odd ones as they are and the even ones reversed.

solutions.title: Walk each diagonal from its clamped start
solutions.idea: Compute the first cell of each diagonal directly and walk it in the right direction, with no buffers.

followups: Read the grid along the other diagonals (row − col constant) without zigzagging. What key do you bucket by?
The grid is a jagged array where rows have different lengths. Which approach still works unchanged?
